one_liner: C++17 multi-format struct serializer whose built-in MsgPack archive saves about 33x and loads about 22x faster than nlohmann::json's MsgPack path.
what_it_does: BitSerializer maps typed C++ objects to JSON, XML, YAML, CSV and MsgPack through one Serialize(archive) method (or a non-intrusive SerializeObject free function) built from KeyValue pairs, with required/optional fields, validators, post-load refiners and support for most std containers, chrono types and std::variant. Calls are SaveObject<Archive>(obj, std::string or std::ostream) and LoadObject<Archive>(obj, data); switching formats means changing the archive type. It is not a JSON DOM library: there is no value tree to query or edit, only typed models.
how_it_is_fast: The built-in MsgPack archive (like CSV and the new built-in JSON archive) is DOM-free: the writer appends type-tagged big-endian values straight into the caller's std::string, and the string reader parses the input in place and hands strings out as std::string_view, so no tree of std::map nodes and heap-allocated keys is built, which is what nlohmann::json's to_msgpack/from_msgpack path requires. Object fields are looked up with a cursor that continues from the previous key and only rewinds and skips (SkipValue) when keys arrive out of order, so loading in write order is a single linear pass. There is no SIMD or other low-level trick; each value still goes through a virtual IMsgPackWriter/IMsgPackReader call, so the gain is purely architectural (no intermediate DOM).
when_to_use: You serialize typed C++ structs to MsgPack today via nlohmann::json (struct to json DOM, then to_msgpack/from_msgpack); the committed report shows 86842 vs 2621 fields/ms on save and 49254 vs 2206 on load for that swap.
One mapping must target several formats (JSON for debugging, MsgPack on the wire, CSV export) with named keys, fields loadable in any order, and versioning by optional or renamed fields.
Loading needs validation and error collection (Required, MaxSize, Email, PhoneNumber, custom validators, refiners) rather than bare parsing.
Large MsgPack, CSV or JSON inputs read from std::istream with bounded memory (built-in archives read in chunks; the RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML wrappers keep the whole document in memory).
Cross-platform C++17 code on Windows, Linux or macOS (x86, x64, arm32, arm64) installed through vcpkg, Conan Center or CMake FetchContent.
when_not_to_use: You need to inspect or edit arbitrary JSON as a tree: there is no DOM type, only struct mapping.

Raw binary throughput matters more than named keys and schema tolerance: positional serializers (zpp::bits, Cap'n Proto) are a different class, and no dedicated MsgPack library (msgpack-c/cpp, glaze, cereal) was ever benchmarked against it, so the README's 'best-in-class' MsgPack claim is unsupported.

JSON, XML or YAML through the RapidJSON, PugiXml or RapidYAML wrappers: the committed report shows them 0-9% slower than the native libraries (RapidJSON load 11149 vs 11957 fields/ms, PugiXml load 13693 vs 15068), never faster; the faster built-in JSON archive is unreleased (master only) and its '40% faster' claim has no committed numbers.
Builds with exceptions disabled: the README states that working without exceptions is not supported, and all errors (type mismatch, overflow, validation) are reported by throwing.
Exchanging MsgPack timestamps before 1970 or after 2514 with other MsgPack implementations (timestamp 96 byte-order bug, see gotchas).

integration.form: static lib (default) or shared lib: each archive (msgpack-archive, csv-archive, json-archive, rapidjson-archive, pugixml-archive, rapidyaml-archive) is a compiled CMake target over a header-only core; the MsgPack docs state it is not header-only
integration.dependencies: none for the built-in MsgPack, CSV and JSON archives; RapidJSON, PugiXml or RapidYAML for the corresponding wrapper archives
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; VS 2019, GCC 8.3+ (CMake warns below 8.3), Clang 8+, AppleClang 12, Clang-cl; CMake 3.10+
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux, macOS on x86, x64, arm32, arm64 and arm64be (README)
integration.thread_safety: not documented (each SaveObject/LoadObject call creates its own archive and reader/writer; no shared mutable state seen in the MsgPack code read)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the MsgPack bytes are standard, so data written by nlohmann::json::to_msgpack loads into a matching struct, but the API is different: nlohmann adl_serializer to_json/from_json code must be rewritten as Serialize() methods, and code that builds or queries nlohmann::json values has no equivalent

gotchas: MsgPack timestamp 96 is written and read in the wrong field order: CMsgPackStringWriter/CMsgPackStreamWriter emit 0xC7 0x0C 0xFF then int64 seconds then nanoseconds, and both readers expect the same, while the MsgPack spec puts the 32-bit nanoseconds before the 64-bit seconds; the unit tests ShouldWriteTimestamp96 and ShouldReadTimestamp96 encode the swapped order. It round-trips with itself but other MsgPack implementations misread std::chrono/time_t values whose seconds are negative or at least 2^34 (pre-1970, post-2514), despite docs/bitserializer_msgpack.md claiming full compliance with the Timestamp extension. This does not touch the benchmark numbers (the test model has no timestamps).

Harness favours the DOM-free side beyond the format work itself: the output std::string is reserved to 16384 bytes and reused across iterations (the 12783-byte MsgPack output never reallocates) and CBasicTestModel's constructor pre-reserves every target string, while the nlohmann path rebuilds a std::map-based DOM per call, grows the std::vector from to_msgpack from empty and then copies it into the std::string (nlohmann's to_msgpack has an output_adapter<char> overload that writes into a std::string directly), and loads via a DOM although nlohmann's sax_parse supports MsgPack. Each figure is the best single run of a cache-hot ~13 KB, 30-object payload (about 3.8 us vs 126 us per save), so the 33x/22x ratios overstate gains on cold, allocation-heavy real workloads.

Out-of-order keys cost a rescan: the object scope searches forward from the last key and rewinds with SkipValue, so loading fields in a different order than they were written turns each lookup into O(fields) skips (README: maximum performance only when loading in the same order).

Streams are much slower than memory buffers: MsgPack save to std::ostream measured 11379 vs 86842 fields/ms to std::string (the stream writer calls put/write per value) and the RapidJSON archive 1045 vs 13636; serialize to a string and write it out in hot paths. The README also requires the application and the compiled archive libraries to share C++ standard, optimisation flags and runtime, so there is no ABI stability.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick BitSerializer over zpp::bits or Cap'n Proto when you need named-key, schema-tolerant formats (MsgPack, JSON, CSV, XML, YAML) from one struct mapping with validation, and over cmp when you want typed C++ struct mapping rather than a low-level C MsgPack API. For JSON throughput specifically, DAW JSON Link and json.cpp carry stronger JSON-specific evidence; BitSerializer's measured win is MsgPack against nlohmann::json only.
verified_claims_summary: First-party report in benchmarks/archives (speed report last updated with the 2026-01-10 chart commit): saving a 30-object, 330-field test model (bool, int8, uint64, float, double and five strings per object) to an in-memory std::string as MsgPack ran at 86842 fields/ms with BitSerializer versus 2621 with nlohmann::json's DOM plus to_msgpack (about 33x, derived from page data), and loading at 49254 versus 2206 fields/ms (about 22x), each the minimum single-run time over a 30 s window after a 10 s CPU warm-up on one pinned core. Compiler, flags, nlohmann version and CPU are not stated; the harness validates the loaded model after each load stage, and the nlohmann JSON-text benchmark class exists but is never run.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-30, v0.85 released 2026-01-11, built-in JSON archive only on master and set to replace the RapidJSON archive), MIT-licensed, 34 stars and 8 forks, packaged in vcpkg and Conan Center; usable now for MsgPack and CSV, but fix or avoid timestamp 96 if other MsgPack readers consume your data.
